court: County Court of New York, Cayuga County
holding_summary: The court held that seven compartments constructed and temporarily tenanted to manufacture additional dwellings for liquor-license consent purposes were not genuine dwellings under the statute. It therefore canceled the liquor tax certificate.

quotes.text: The legislative intent, no doubt, was that the consents required before a certificate could be issued to traffic in liquors at a place located in the midst of residences should be consents of owners of buildings occupied exclusively and' in good faith as dwellings, and should not include buildings .constructed, used and occupied as dwellings merely as a pretense and a show; not buildings constructed and tenanted temporarily, and for the purpose of evading the law.

the seven divisions of the .buildings upon the rear of the premises of Mr. Koenig, whose consent was filed with the application as owner of. seven buildings occupied as dwellings, are not dwellings within the meaning of the law, and should not be counted as such.

After a careful consideration of the evidence submitted, and of what appears to me to he the purpose, effect and intent of the Liquor Tax Law, I determine that the application for the cancellation of the certificate should be granted.

notes: The occupants changed frequently and some remained only a short time, but the opinion gives no precise duration or clear evidence that Koenig charged them for occupancy.
The reference to transient hotel guests appears only in allegations supporting resubmission of local liquor-option questions; the holding concerns election procedures and voter qualifications.

holding_summary: The court permitted police to post officers outside and inspect a licensed hotel, but enjoined them from warning prospective customers that it was a disorderly house and threatening possible raids and arrests.

quotes.text: The motion will be denied so far as it seeks to obtain an injunction preventing the posting of officers and inspection of the premises, and granted so far as it relates to the interference with proposed customers by volunteered statements and threats.

notes: The premises contained thirty-two furnished rooms for lodgers, but the court did not adjudicate whether an occupant's interest was a lease, license, or other lodging status.

cite: Sautter v. Utica City National Bank, 45 Misc. 15
notes: The case concerns municipal authorization of building columns projecting into a sidewalk, not compensated occupancy or lodging.

cite: S. Liebmann's Sons Brewing Co. v. De Nicolo, 46 Misc. 268
court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: This commercial landlord-tenant dispute concerns unpaid rent, a liquor-license agreement, and an improper counterclaim, without lodging or short-term dwelling occupancy.
The case enforces a residential-use covenant against a vaudeville theater and liquor business, not against compensated residential occupancy.
The case concerns surrender of an ordinary one-year lease of an entire house and does not address lodging, boarding, or short-term letting.

holding_summary: The restrictive covenant did not prohibit operating a private hotel or boarding house for regular guests who lodged and took meals there. It did prohibit an independent annex operated solely as a restaurant and drinking saloon open indiscriminately to the public.

quotes.text: Proof of the existence of hotels or boarding-houses of the character above referred to does not establish a breach of such covenant. Murray v. Charman, supra.

Down to about June, 1905, the defendant had used the premises owned by her for a private hotel or boarding-house for the entertainment of gentlemen and their families, who> desired to spend the heated term in the country. The large majority of the patrons of the house were permanent guests who not only lodged and took their meals there, but remained for a considerable period of time.

The plaintiff is therefore entitled to a judgment again.-1 the defendant, Harriet E. Mitchell, perpetually enjoining- and restraining her and her servants, agents, and all persons claiming through or under her, from carrying on upon the premises owned by her the business of a restaurant, or saloon for the sale of intoxicating liquors, or from carrying on upon the said premises the business of furnishing and-selling to-, persons indiscriminately food or liquor, or from furnishing: or selling to any person either food or liquor; except to persons who are regular guests of a private hotel or boardinghouse carried on upon said premises, or their invited friends, such liquors to be served only to such guests with their meals or in their private rooms.

notes: The months classification is inferred from the described summer-season operation, permanent guests, and stays for a considerable period; no exact stay length is stated.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: The case concerns a broker's failure to prove entitlement to a commission for procuring an unidentified tenant, with no evidence of residential or lodging use.
The case restrains conversion of a private residence to stores and offices and does not address letting rooms or dwellings for residential occupancy.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: The case concerns the preclusive effect of a rent judgment on whether an unspecified tenancy was monthly or yearly; the premises and use are not identified as dwelling or lodging accommodations.

cite: Salmon v. M. E. Blasier Manufacturing Co., 53 Misc. 36
notes: The plaintiff's boarding-house business is mentioned only as an element of alleged trespass damages; the decision concerns pleading requirements for treble damages.

notes: The case concerns an assignee landlord's right to treat a commercial holdover as a renewed annual tenancy, not lodging or short-term dwelling occupancy.
The proceeding interprets liquor-license distance, dwelling-count, agency, and taxpayer provisions without addressing lodging or compensated residential occupancy.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: This is a streetcar-collision negligence case with no connection to property letting or lodging.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
notes: Although the facts describe hotel guests leaving damaged rooms, the holding concerns constructive eviction under a five-year commercial lease and does not decide guests' occupancy rights or lodging regulation.
The court held that a two-family house was residential rather than legally objectionable, but the case contains no facts about compensated occupancy, letting, or duration.
The references to collecting rents and making leases concern proof of adverse possession among cotenants, not the character or regulation of lodging occupancy.
